newsitem.title: FRANCE: President defends Algeria's human rights record.
newsitem.headline: President defends Algeria's human rights record.

text.p: Algerian President Liamine Zeroual, defending his government's policy on human rights, on Tuesday said his country was open for dialogue on the issue but would not accept outside interference under the cover of human rights advocacy.

The London-based human rights group Amnesty International in November condemned both Algeria's security forces and Moslem guerrillas for what it called widescale human rights abuses in the five-year-old fighting in the North African country.

"Algeria is a country open for a frank dialogue on the question of human rights but it rejects any attempt at meddling in its internal affairs under the cover of the defence of human rights," said Zeroual.

Zeroual was quoted by the official Algerian news agency APS in an address to the government-appointed human rights watchdog, Human Rights National Observatory, after Kamel Rezzag Bara was reappointed as head of the group.

"The dissolution of special courts, the lifting of the curfew across the country and the shutting of administrative detention centres constitute measures proving the willingness of the authorities to eliminate all obstacles in the way of setting up a state of law," said Zeroual.

Zeroual had closed Saharan desert detention camps in 1995 freeing hundreds of Moslem militants held without trial after the authorities imposed a state of emergency early in 1992. The curfew was also lifted in 1995 and the courts dissolved a year earlier.

Amnesty said in its last report that "despite repeated claims by the authorities that human rights are respected and that the security situation has improved, the fact that the pattern of abuses continues shows that for both security forces and armed opposition groups human rights abuses are an integral part of their strategy".

Zeroual did not mention Amnesty by name when he referred to what he called outside interference. But the authorities earlier faulted the Amnesty report as biased, saying it equated members of the security forces -- defending Algerians -- with "terrorist" groups.
About 60,000 people, many of them civilians, have died in Algeria's violence since early 1992 when the authorities cancelled a general election in which radical Islamists had taken a commanding lead.
